answer.recommendation: Aim for about 1.62 g per kg of body weight per day of total protein while resistance training in a deficit, since a meta-analysis found no further fat-free mass gain beyond that [1]. Going higher, up to 2.4 g/kg/day, is plausible in a steep deficit but unproven, resting on one small low-grade trial [2].
answer.why: A meta-analysis of 49 randomized trials (n=1863) found a breakpoint at 1.62 g/kg/day of total protein, beyond which there was no additional fat-free mass gain [1]. That evidence is high grade but indirect, because it was not restricted to energy restriction and effects were smaller in older and untrained individuals [1]. The only deficit trial (n=40, 4 weeks, 40% deficit) found lean mass +1.2 kg at 2.4 g/kg/day versus +0.1 kg at 1.2 g/kg/day [2]. That trial is low grade and compared only two intakes, so it cannot locate a plateau [3]. Its lower intake of 1.2 g/kg/day sits below the meta-analytic breakpoint of 1.62 g/kg/day, so the two do not clearly conflict [1][2]. Confidence is low because the evidence is indirect and the deficit data are sparse [4].

positions.stance: Total protein of about 1.62 g/kg/day is enough, with no further gain in fat-free mass beyond that
positions.best_counterargument: The meta-analysis was not restricted to an energy deficit and mostly studied untrained people. The only deficit trial found a 1.2 kg lean mass gain at 2.4 g/kg/day versus 0.1 kg at 1.2 g/kg/day, so a higher intake may help during dieting.

answer.what_would_change_this: Larger trials in resistance-trained people in an energy deficit that test several protein intakes, including above 1.62 g/kg/day, could move the plateau up or confirm it [5]. A replication of the 2.4 g/kg/day result over a longer period would also shift the advice [3].
answer.applies_to_you: You are an intermediate male lifter at 80 kg cutting, so the target is expressed per kg of your body weight, as 1.62 g/kg/day [1]. The meta-analysis mixed ages and training status and did not evaluate energy deficit size, so it only partly matches your situation [5]. The deficit trial used overweight young men (BMI 25-30) who were not specified as resistance-trained, so it may not match you either [4].
answer.practical_protocol: Next week, set daily protein at about 1.62 g/kg/day of total protein and keep resistance training in place [1]. If your deficit is steep, you could test a somewhat higher intake, with 2.4 g/kg/day as the highest level studied in a deficit [2]. Track strength and body measurements to see how you respond.
answer.disclaimer: This is general, evidence-based training and nutrition information, not medical advice. Talk to a doctor or registered dietitian before making changes if you have a health condition, injury, or take medication.

verdict.rationale: The only credible position rests on the 2018 meta-analysis of 49 RCTs (n=1863), which found a breakpoint at 1.62 g/kg/day with no further fat-free mass gain beyond it. That evidence is high grade but indirect: it mostly covers resistance training without an energy deficit and includes untrained people, so it is down-weighted for this intermediate lifter on a fat loss phase. The higher-protein side is right that deficits may raise needs, so a modest margin above 1.6 g/kg/day is reasonable. The evidence is indirect and sparse, so confidence is low and the status is leaning rather than consensus.
